claims.text: Resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion in high-entropy alloys is predominantly governed by the dynamic formation and continual regeneration of a mechanically robust, self-healing amorphous oxide film.
Synergistic interactions among multiple alloying elements produce the protective amorphous oxide film.
Lattice distortion caused by multiple alloying elements contributes to high hardness.
Multiple reactive alloying elements contribute to chemical passivation.
Chromium and aluminum are reactive elements known to form passivating oxides in the proposed alloy context.
Mechanical abrasion periodically removes the superficial oxide layer.
An optimal balance of reactive passivating elements promotes rapid reformation of a chemically protective oxide film after abrasion.
Rapid oxide-film regeneration minimizes abrasive wear.
Rapid oxide-film regeneration minimizes corrosive attack.

An alloy optimized for passivating-element synergy will have a significantly lower overall degradation rate during simultaneous wear and corrosion than a compositionally matched control lacking that synergy.
The optimized alloy will develop smaller wear scars than the control.
The optimized alloy will exhibit lower corrosion-pit density than the control.
The optimized alloy will exhibit less cumulative material loss than the control.
The protective effect should persist under moderate mechanical loads and corrosive conditions when oxide regeneration can keep pace with oxide removal.
Very high mechanical stresses can cause oxide removal to outpace regeneration and defeat the proposed mechanism.
Highly acidic or chloride-rich environments can prevent oxide regeneration from keeping pace with damage and cause the mechanism to fail.
Temperature and pH may influence the efficacy of oxide-film regeneration.
